source.title: Do Methods to Jailbreak and Defend LLMs Generalize Across Languages?
source.authors: B. Atil; R. Passonneau; Fred Morstatter

record.tranche_reason: The study applies an adversarial jailbreak that uses refusal-avoiding rules, suffixes, and optimization toward a compliant first token, then measures harmful-response rates across models and languages. This conceptually tests whether such attacks bypass refusal, but it does not measure the original claim’s fine-tuning or token-position KL effects.
record.gate_note: Only the Andriushchenko et al. (2025) attack is recorded below for V4. The attack includes adversarial suffixes and optimization to raise the probability of the first token being “sure”; it does not prefill compliant tokens or change decoding. Logic-jailbreak results are not rows for V4 because that method does not test getting past a compliant opening. Standard-query rates are recorded as the baseline for each attack result.
record.test_reason: The study applies Andriushchenko et al.'s prompt attack across 10 languages and 6 models on HarmBench and AdvBench. The attack combines refusal-avoiding rules, adversarial suffixes and optimization toward a 'sure' first token, and the study reports unsafe-rate changes against standard queries. That bears on V4 (suffix or opening attacks defeat refusal) in a new multilingual setting, so T3 rather than T2. There is no fine-tuning, per-token KL, parameter localization or deepening training, so V1–V3 and V5–V7 are not tested.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly right. The authors also conclude that high-resource languages are safer under standard queries but more vulnerable to jailbreaks. They further find that simple defenses (self-verification prompting, lightweight classifiers) help but depend on language and model.
record.recipe_differences: This is a multilingual jailbreak evaluation, not the fine-tuning or per-token KL procedure in the source claims. It applies an existing attack with refusal-avoiding rules, adversarial suffixes, and first-token optimization; the paper adapts it across languages. It tests neither prefilling nor decoding changes.
record.method_sensitivity: Unsafe response rates vary substantially by model and language. The paper also reports different results across HarmBench and AdvBench, although AdvBench attack cells are not extracted here.

fits_no_version.finding: The logic-expression jailbreak (rewriting harmful queries as formal logic) raises unsafe rates for most models, e.g. GPT-4o English 4→61, but barely affects Sonnet 4. It does not target the response opening.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Out-of-distribution reformulation of harmful queries (formal logic) bypasses refusal independent of the opening tokens.

fits_no_version.finding: High-resource languages are safer under standard queries but relatively more vulnerable under jailbreaks.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Jailbreak vulnerability scales with language proficiency, reversing the standard-query resource gradient.

record.problems: Unsafe response rates are judged by GPT-4o; the paper notes that invalid responses are excluded from the reported unsafe rates. Native-speaker annotation sampled 100 examples per language, but the paper reports no uncertainty estimates for the tabled unsafe rates. Results cover 10 languages and six models. AdvBench results are not included in the extracted rows.
record.rows_left_out: Table 3 AdvBench unsafe-rate cells for Andrius25 and standard prompts, and all Logic-jailbreak cells, are omitted to stay within the 60-row limit while retaining the full HarmBench Andrius25 model-by-language table, including its reversals and partial effects. The omitted tabled results also vary across datasets; no aggregate or representative value is substituted.

untested.parts: Prefilling of compliant response tokens and decoding changes are not tested. The attack is a single fixed prompt optimized for GPT-4o and transferred to the other models, and no first-token or position-level analysis is done.
No per-token KL or position analysis.
No test of the cause of shallowness.

record.verdict_notes: The AdvBench Andrius25 cells (Table 3) are declared omitted. They show the same pattern: open models near 100%, little effect on GPT-4o Spanish/Turkish (0.19→1.92/2.88) and none on Sonnet English (0.38→0.19). Unsafe rates come from a GPT-4o judge with invalid responses excluded, and no uncertainty is reported. The attack prompt was optimized for GPT-4o, yet it transfers far better to the open models than it works on GPT-4o itself.

versions.untested_parts: No fine-tuning on harmful examples or post-fine-tuning harmful-compliance measurement.
No fine-tuning on ordinary or selected benign data.
No per-token KL or other measurement of aligned-versus-base response-position differences.

Tests an adversarial prompt method with suffixes and first-token optimization. Does not test prefilled compliant tokens or decoding changes; results are reported for HarmBench in the extracted rows, not AdvBench.
No localization, ablation, or editing of safety-related parameters or ranks.
No test of whether training data or objective causes safety shallowness.
No training that deepens safety across response positions, or evaluation of whether such training holds up.

relationships.condition: Open-weight models (Qwen2.5-7b/14b, Llama3.1-8b/70b) in most languages, plus GPT-4o and Sonnet 4 in some languages, HarmBench
relationships.reason: Unsafe rates jump from low baselines to roughly 70–99.5%. Examples: Qwen14b English 2.0→99.5, Llama8b English 6.0→94.5, GPT-4o Bengali 8.0→82.0, Sonnet 4 Chinese 4.0→45.0.
relationships.display_finding: Open-model unsafe rates in most languages jumped from low baselines to roughly 70–99.5%, e.g. Qwen 14B in English from 2.0 to 99.5 and Llama 8B in English from 6.0 to 94.5, while GPT-4o in Bengali went from 8.0 to 82.0 and Sonnet 4 in Chinese only from 4.0 to 45.0.
